svg.title: Multicast bandwidth arithmetic: stream times branches times one plus redundancy, measured where the copies are made
svg.desc: The formula at the top: budget equals stream bit rate times branches times one plus the redundancy factor, plus headroom. Three panels show where the multiplication happens. In the Layer 3 core one packet on one link serves every downstream branch, so core cost is the stream rate per link joining the tree. On a Layer 2 access switch the packet is copied per port, so 8 Mbps times 24 ports is 192 Mbps of egress. On the WAN only sites that joined receive a copy, so two sites out of two hundred cost two copies. A worked example follows: 8 Mbps, 24 branches, live-live 1+1 and 30 percent headroom gives 499 Mbps of reserved capacity, against a naive 8 Mbps plan - a 62x underestimate.
svg.text: Capacity is not the stream bit rate
Multiply at the copy points. Then add redundancy. Then add headroom. Anything less is a guess that fails at the first big event.
budget = stream rate x branches x (1 + redundancy) x (1 + headroom)
"branches" means copy points, not viewers: a Layer 3 node copies once per outgoing link, a Layer 2 switch once per outgoing port.
One copy per link on the tree
The core carries the stream once per
direction, no matter how many receivers
Core cost = stream x links in the tree
The uplink is fine and the access port
Cost = stream x ports that joined
Multicast saves WAN bandwidth only for
the sites with no receiver. A site with one
viewer costs the same as unicast.
Cost = stream x sites that joined
WORKED EXAMPLE: ONE 8 MBPS CHANNEL, 24 BRANCHES, LIVE-LIVE PROTECTION, 30% HEADROOM

Multicast saves bandwidth on links with no receivers. It never saves bandwidth on a link with many: those are exactly the links where replication multiplies.
